title: Al-Malik, the King
hookLine: the King, owner of everything, and so nothing is really yours

lines: CAN YOU REFUSE TO RETURN A LOAN?
cards: A library book can go everywhere with a person for three weeks. It gets read in bed and on the bus, a corner folded with a twinge of guilt. It starts to feel like theirs.

Then the due date comes, and it goes back, because it never was. In Medina, a woman named Umm Sulaym lost her little son while her husband, Abu Talha, was away. When he came home, she fed him and let him rest.
Then, Sahih Muslim reports, she asked him: if people lent something to a family, and then asked for it back, would the family have the right to refuse?

teach.h: SEEK YOUR REWARD FOR YOUR SON.
teach.b: No, said Abu Talha. Then, she said, seek your reward with Allah for your son. He was upset that she had waited to tell him, and he went to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, who prayed for blessing on the two of them.
Al-Malik comes from the root m-l-k: to own, to possess, to rule. The same root gives malik, king, and mulk, sovereignty.
In the Fatiha, one line has two accepted readings: Maliki yawm id-din, King of the Day of Judgment, and Maaliki, Owner of it. Both are recited, the meanings held together.
The Qur'an names Him al-Malik in al-Hashr; Pickthall has: He is Allah, than Whom there is no other God, the Sovereign Lord. And in an-Nas, the King of mankind.
Bukhari and Muslim record the Prophet describing the Day when Allah will fold up the heavens, take the earth in His hand, and say: I am the King.

teach.h: WHERE ARE THE KINGS OF THE EARTH?
teach.b: Where are the kings of the earth? Every crown and title, gone quiet.

teach.h: WHAT'S MINE IS HELD ON LOAN.
teach.b: If He is the Owner, what a person calls mine is held on loan: the house, the phone, the body, even the children they love. That doesn't make things cheap; a borrowed thing is treated with care.
It loosens the grip. At any loss, Muslims say words from al-Baqarah that Pickthall renders: Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning.
This week began with the beautiful names, the name of names, and mercy vast and near. It ends with the King.

how: Muslims say inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un (we belong to Allah and to Him we return) at news of any loss, from a death to a broken cup, and wealth, family and life are often spoken of as an amanah, a trust held for a time.

o: the Owner and Ruler of everything there is
an earthly king who rules in God's name
a ruler the people choose by vote

games.q: what's inside the name — tap the pairs.
p: to own, to possess, to rule

s: the Fatiha's line about the Day has only one accepted reading
two: Maliki, King, and Maaliki, Owner. both are recited.
Muslims say we are Allah's and to Him we return only at a death
it's said at any loss, great or small.
a hadith pictures Allah asking, where are the kings of the earth?

games.q: Umm Sulaym asks her husband: if something lent is asked back, may the family refuse? what does he say?
o: yes, if they've grown to love it
only if they're paid for it
games.why: no. then she told him their son had died, and to seek his reward with Allah. the Prophet prayed for blessing on them (Muslim).

practice: Hold something small you think of as yours, your phone, your keys, a ring, a cup, in your open hand, and say quietly: this is lent to me, noticing what stirs in your chest, resistance or relief.
Then set it down gently, rest your hands on your knees, and notice that your hands are lent too. If you pray, you can say inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un.

wordCard.voice: Al-Malik. The King, the Owner of everything, so that all we hold is lent, to be cared for and one day returned. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the King, from m-l-k, to own and to rule.

carryVoice: Your line: everything is lent. Hold it like a library book. That's a week of names.

sources.q: He is Allah, than Whom there is no other God, the Sovereign Lord,
Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning.

sources.ref: Qur'an 1:4 (Maliki / Maaliki yawm id-din); 114:2 (the King of mankind)
Sahih Muslim 2144 (Umm Sulaym and Abu Talha)
Sahih al-Bukhari 4812; Sahih Muslim 2787 (I am the King; where are the kings of the earth?)
